title: Charting the Information and Misinformation Landscape to Characterize Misinfodemics on Social Media: COVID-19 Infodemiology Study at a Planetary Scale
screen_reason: Infodemiology study of a 1% Twitter stream filtered on COVID-19 keywords, release v2.45 = 1,443,871,621 tweets from 21 January 2020 to 30 April 2021. The authors isolated every tweet carrying a URL from a domain listed by Media Bias/Fact Check as conspiracy-pseudoscience or questionable, giving a misinformation subset of 12,689,165 tweets. Both counts are stated verbatim and the subset is drawn from that exact corpus, so the share (0.88%) is an exact part/whole from verbatim counts and is keepable under R8. The rest of the paper (topic models, narratives, retweet-network clustering, echo chambers) reports no other share with a misinformation numerator and a stated denominator.

estimates.country: Not stated; worldwide Twitter stream filtered on English-language COVID-19 keywords
estimates.measure_type: % of collected COVID-19 tweets that carried a URL from a conspiracy-pseudoscience or questionable domain (Media Bias/Fact Check)
estimates.denominator: 1,443,871,621 COVID-19-related tweets collected in real time from Twitter's 1% streaming API using a manually curated English keyword list, 21 January 2020 - 30 April 2021
estimates.definition: Tweet contains a URL whose domain is on the Media Bias/Fact Check conspiracy-pseudoscience list or questionable-sources list
estimates.misinfo_def: "a URL belonging to a domain that has been determined to be prone to publish questionable or conspiracy-pseudoscience-related content according to the third-party service Media Bias/Fact Check (MBFC)"; MBFC classes a domain as conspiracy-pseudoscience if it "may publish" such content, and questionable sources "exhibit one or more of" a set of listed problems
estimates.source_quote: This resulted in a COVID-19 misinformation data subset totaling 12,689,165 tweets.
estimates.page_loc: Methods, 'Data' p. 2 and 'Identifying Conspiratorial, Questionable, and Random Sources' p. 5; Abstract Results
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Media Bias/Fact Check, a third-party rating service, supplied two domain lists: conspiracy-pseudoscience sources and questionable sources. No inter-rater reliability or independent validation of the lists is reported; the authors describe the criteria as permissive ('may publish', 'exhibit one or more of').
estimates.moderator_quote: We leveraged release v2.45 for this paper, which contains 1,443,871,621 tweets from January 21, 2020, through April 30, 2021.
estimates.notes: The paper never states this percentage; it is computed from two verbatim counts on the same corpus (allowed under R8). The denominator is ALL COVID-19 tweets, the great majority of which carry no URL at all, so this value is much lower than studies whose denominator is URL-carrying tweets only; it is not comparable to link-level shares without that caveat. Coded SHARING (content_share) rather than CONTENT because the paper frames the corpus as content people shared ('the volume of information shared from conspiracy, questionable, and random sources') and the instructions put '% of shared links unreliable' under SHARING. breadth is blank per the source-level-list rule. classification_level=source_level: no claim was checked, only the publishing domain.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) '13% of the 737,722 users tagged for engaging in these 3 topics' discussed all three narratives - computed inside the misinformation subset and describing narrative overlap, not misinformation prevalence, so no row. (b) The daily increases in unreliable URLs (conspiratorial 4.47, questionable 5.69 per day, P<.001) are regression coefficients on volume, not shares. (c) 'The prevalence of information shared from unreliable sources is known to be high on Twitter and can reach up to 40% depending on the classification criteria [72]' is a figure the paper cites from elsewhere; R8 forbids keeping it. (d) Table 2's language shares (English 64.29% etc.) describe the corpus, not misinformation. (e) The topic-cluster share 'around 10% of all tweets' refers to a general discussion topic, not misinformation. (f) Average clustering coefficients (66.2 for the questionable-sources network) and the network analyses are structural, not prevalence. No CONCENTRATION row is possible: the paper never pairs a top-X% group with its share of activity, so R1 is not satisfied.

rob.design: Observational computational study of a public COVID-19 Twitter archive. Frame: Twitter 1% streaming API, filtered by a manually curated English-only keyword list, collected in real time from 21 January 2020; release v2.45 used here contains 1,443,871,621 tweets through 30 April 2021. IRB-approved (USC UP-17-00610, UP-21-00005). Misinformation identification is entirely source-level: any tweet with a URL on the MBFC conspiracy-pseudoscience or questionable list. No claim-level verification, no human coding of tweets, no reliability statistics. The authors flag the 1% sampling rate and the English-only keyword list as limitations. Additional analyses used a matched design of three 250-domain sets (conspiracy, questionable, random). The misinformation subset is a convenience proxy: the authors state explicitly that a user in it did not necessarily share such content exclusively or mostly.
rob.item6_quote: We created a subset of our data set for published tweets that contain a URL belonging to a domain that has been determined to be prone to publish questionable or conspiracy-pseudoscience–related content according to the third-party service Media Bias/Fact Check (MBFC) [17]. We used this as a proxy to identify users who have engaged with misinformation.
